summary: Defines the format for writing literal IPv6 addresses inside URLs, for use in web browsers. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level, and it was replaced by RFC 3986.

plainLanguage.summary: Since colons already separate parts of web addresses, long IPv6 numbers need a special wrapper so browsers do not get confused.

questions: how to write an ipv6 address in a url
why are ipv6 addresses in brackets in urls
why are ipv6 addresses in square brackets
what changed in rfc 2396 for ipv6
subtitle: Square brackets let an IPv6 address sit inside a URL without its colons being misread.

tldr.problem: The text form of an IPv6 address uses ":" and "." as delimiters, just like URLs, so a literal IPv6 address cannot be dropped into a URL directly.
tldr.mechanism: The address is enclosed in "[" and "]", and the URI host syntax of RFC 2396 is changed to accept this form while making the brackets reserved characters.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2732 has been obsoleted by RFC 3986, which now carries the bracketed IPv6 literal syntax.

today: RFC 2732 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 3986, so that is the place to look for the current URI syntax. It updated RFC 2396.

sections.title: The Clash Between IPv6 and URLs
sections.content:
The textual form of a literal IPv6 address is not directly compatible with URLs, because both use : and . as delimiters. The goal of this RFC is a format that allows easy cut and paste of the address with a minimum of editing.

Web browsers SHOULD implement the format. Other applications and protocols that use URLs MAY use it. The RFC says it had been implemented in IPv6 versions of several widely deployed browsers, including Microsoft Internet Explorer, Mozilla and Lynx.
sections.plainLanguage: A web address and a long number both use colons, so they get tangled. This memo untangles them.

sections.title: The Bracket Syntax
sections.content:
To use a literal IPv6 address in a URL, enclose it in [ and ]. For example, 1080::8:800:200C:417A becomes http://[1080::8:800:200C:417A]/foo. A port still goes after the closing bracket, as in http://[FEDC:BA98:7654:3210:FEDC:BA98:7654:3210]:80/index.html.

The RFC also shows address forms with an embedded IPv4 part, such as http://[::192.9.5.5]/ipng.
sections.plainLanguage: Wrap the long number in square brackets, then add the rest of the web address after it.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 2396
sections.content:
The RFC updates the generic URI syntax of RFC 2396 in three ways.

  • The host rule gains an option: host = hostname | IPv4address | IPv6reference, where ipv6reference = "[" IPv6address "]" and IPv6address comes from RFC 2373.
  • The IPv4address definition is replaced with the RFC 2373 one, which allows at most three decimal digits per segment.
  • [ and ] are added to the reserved set and removed from the unwise set.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rulebook said square brackets were not allowed in web addresses. The new rule says they are allowed, but only for this one job.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The RFC says that representing literal IPv6 addresses this way does not introduce any known new security concerns. Its IANA Considerations section says only "None".
sections.plainLanguage: Adding brackets does not make anything less safe, as far as anyone knew, and nothing needed to be registered.

references.text: Hinden, R. and S. Deering, "IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture", RFC 2373, July 1998.
Fielding, R., Masinter, L. and T. Berners-Lee, "Uniform Resource Identifiers: Generic Syntax", RFC 2396, August 1998.
